---
title: Quarto Academic Typst
subtitle: A minimalistic Quarto + Typst template for academic writing
author:
  - name: Kazuharu Yanagimoto
    email: kazuharu.yanagimoto@cemfi.edu.es
    orcid: 0009-0007-1967-8304
    affiliations:
      - name: CEMFI
abstract: |
  {{< lipsum 1 >}}
thanks: |
  You can write acknowledgements here.
keywords:
  - Quarto
  - Typst
  - format
date: today
date-format: full
bibliography: references.bib
format:
  academic-typst:
    section-numbering: "1.1.1"
execute:
  echo: false
---

This document shows a minimal example of the template. For more information, see the [full demo](https://kazuyanagimoto.com/quarto-academic-typst/template-full.pdf) and its [source](https://github.com/kazuyanagimoto/quarto-academic-typst/blob/main/template-full.qmd).

# Section as Heading Level 1

Section numbering can be specified in the YAML `section-numbering` field as other Typst templates.

## Subsection as Heading Level 2

You can use LaTeX math expressions:

$$
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \sum_{k \neq -1} \tau_h \mathbb{1}\{E_i + k = t\} +
\varepsilon_{it}.
$$

### Subsubsection as Heading Level 3

I don't use and don't recommend using heading levels 3 and below but it works.

## Citation

You can cite a reference like this [@katsushika1831] or @horst2020. Typst has some built-in citation styles. Check the [Typst documentation](https://typst.app/docs/reference/model/bibliography/#parameters-style) for more information.

# Figures and Tables

## Figures

As @fig-hist-mpg shows, the caption is displayed below the figure. As a caption of the figure (`fig-cap`), I use bold text for the title and use a normal text for the description.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist-mpg
#| fig-cap: "**Histogram of Miles per Gallon**. The x-axis shows the miles per gallon, and the y-axis shows the frequency."

hist(mtcars$mpg)
```

## Tables

You can use [tinytable](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/tinytable/) for general tables and [modelsummary](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/modelsummary/) for regression tables.[^1] As @tbl-mtcars-head shows, the caption is displayed above the table. The notes of the table can be added using the `notes` argument of the `tinytable::tt()` function.

[^1]: Since the default backend of `modelsummary` is `tinytable`, you can use the customization options of `tinytable` for `modelsummary`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mtcars-head
#| tbl-cap: Head of the mtcars Dataset

nt <- "_Notes_: This table shows the first six rows of the mtcars dataset."
mtcars[1:5, 1:5] |>
  tinytable::tt(width = 0.8, notes = nt)         
```

# Last words

I made this template for my working papers, so it may not be suitable for other fields than economics. I am happy to receive feedback and suggestions for improvement.

{{< appendix >}}

# Supplemental Figures

The figure numbering will be reset to "A.1", "A.2", etc so that it is clear that these figures are part of the appendix.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter-car
#| fig-cap: "**Scatter Plot of Car Data**. The x-axis shows the weight of the car, and the y-axis shows the miles per gallon."

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
```

# 1. Base pumpkin data (approximate curved segments using parametric or smooth paths)
t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
pumpkin_df <- data.frame(
  x = 1.5 * cos(t),
  y = 1.0 * sin(t)
)

# 2. Facial features (triangles for eyes/nose, polygon for smile)
eyes <- data.frame(
  x = c(-0.5, -0.7, -0.3, 0.3, 0.7, 0.5),
  y = c(0.4, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.4),
  group = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2)
)

nose <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, -0.15, 0.15),
  y = c(0, -0.2, -0.2)
)

mouth <- data.frame(
  x = c(-0.6, 0.6, 0.4, 0, -0.4),
  y = c(-0.3, -0.3, -0.5, -0.6, -0.5)
)

# 3. Plotting the scene
ggplot() +
  # Pumpkin body
  geom_polygon(data = pumpkin_df, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "darkorange", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  # Stem
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = -0.15, xmax = 0.15, ymin = 1.0, ymax = 1.3), fill = "forestgreen", color = "black") +
  # Eyes
  geom_polygon(data = eyes, aes(x = x, y = y, group = group), fill = "gold", color = "black") +
  # Nose
  geom_polygon(data = nose, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "gold", color = "black") +
  # Mouth
  geom_polygon(data = mouth, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "gold", color = "black") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void()

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

#' Ghost plotting function
#' @param ghost_df Data frame with x and y coordinates of the ghost shape
#' @param ghost_color Color of the ghost (default is neon green)
#' @return ggplot object of the ghost
plot_simple_ghost <- function(ghost_df, ghost_color = "#39FF14") {
  x_center <- mean(range(ghost_df$x))
  y_top <- max(ghost_df$y)
  y_bottom <- min(ghost_df$y)
  ghost_height <- y_top - y_bottom
  ghost_width <- diff(range(ghost_df$x))
  
  # Eyes
  eye_y <- y_bottom + .7 * ghost_height        
  eye_x <- x_center + c(-0.06, 0.06) * ghost_width
  eyes <- data.frame(x = eye_x, y = rep(eye_y, 2))
  
  # Mouth: several waves 
  mouth_width <- ghost_width * 0.4
  mouth_x <- seq(x_center - 0.3 * mouth_width, x_center + 0.3 * mouth_width, length.out = 80)
  mouth_y <- y_bottom + 0.55 * ghost_height + sin(seq(0, 7 * pi, length.out = 80)) * 0.04 * ghost_height
  mouth <- data.frame(x = mouth_x, y = mouth_y)
  
  # 8 neon glow layers
  glow_layers <- data.frame(
    linewidth = c(12, 10, 8, 6, 4.5, 3, 2, 1),
    alpha = c(0.04, 0.06, 0.09, 0.13, 0.18, 0.25, 0.35, 0.5)
  )
  
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_polygon(
      data = ghost_df, aes(x, y),
      fill = ghost_color, alpha = 0.15, color = NA
    )
  
  # Glow layers for outline, eyes, and mouth
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(glow_layers))) {
    p <- p +
      geom_polygon(
        data = ghost_df, aes(x, y),
        fill = NA, color = scales::alpha(ghost_color, glow_layers$alpha[i]),
        linewidth = glow_layers$linewidth[i]
      ) +
      geom_point(
        data = eyes, aes(x, y),
        color = scales::alpha(ghost_color, glow_layers$alpha[i]),
        size = glow_layers$linewidth[i] * 2.1  ## 1.1
      ) +
      geom_path(
        data = mouth, aes(x, y),
        color = scales::alpha(ghost_color, glow_layers$alpha[i]),
        linewidth = glow_layers$linewidth[i]
      )
  }
  
  # Solid black mouth and eyes
  p <- p +
    geom_path(
      data = mouth, aes(x, y),
      color = "#66ff00", linewidth = 1.2  ## with green ghost
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = eyes, aes(x, y),
      color = "#66ff00",
      size = 2
    ) 
  
  # Fix aspect ratio and theme
  p + 
    coord_fixed(
      xlim = c(-4, 4), 
      ylim = c(-3, 8), 
      expand = TRUE
    ) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA)
    )
}

#' Generate a random ghost shape
#' @param seed Optional seed for reproducibility
#' @return Data frame with x and y coordinates of the ghost shape
ghost_shape <- function(seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  width <- sample(seq(0.5, 3, length.out = 6), 1)  
  height <- sample(1:6,1) 
  x <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 100) * width
  amp <- runif(1, 0.15, 0.28)
  freq <- sample(3:7, 1)
  phase <- runif(1, 0, 2*pi)
  y_top <- sqrt(1 - (x/width)^2) * height + runif(1, -0.03, 0.03)
  y_bottom <- -0.5 * height + sin(seq(0, freq * pi, length.out = 100) + phase) * amp * height
  data.frame(
    x = c(x, rev(x)),
    y = c(y_top, rev(y_bottom))
  )
}

Quarto version 1.10.18

The strongest option for Quarto + RevealJS + results going into a database you control is the dedicated Quarto extension quarto-revealjs-live-questions. Several other viable paths exist (custom forms + Supabase/Firebase, older RevealJS plugins, or commercial embeds).

1. Recommended: quarto-revealjs-live-questions (best fit)
This Quarto extension keeps the questions in your .qmd file and backs them with a small self-hosted server.
Features - Polls and quizzes (mark correct answers with - [x]) - Word clouds (with limits and presenter moderation) - Rating scales / Likert - Live results on the slide (or hidden until you reveal them) - Audience joins once via QR code; a phone-friendly page follows the deck as you advance - Static fallback (plain lists) for PDF or when the server is offline
Storage / database - Cloudflare Workers + Durable Objects (SQLite per session; free tier friendly) - Or Docker (Node.js + JSON files per session on a volume) - Export all results via API (Bearer token): bash   curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <PRESENTER_KEY>" \     https://your-server/api/s/<session>/export - Presenter controls (open/close, reveal answers, reset) via a key in the URL
Quick start
quarto add seandavi/quarto-revealjs-live-questions
In your document:
filters:
  - live-questions
revealjs-plugins:
  - live-questions
live-questions:
  server: https://your-server.workers.dev   # or your Docker host
  session: my-talk-2026
  results: live
  qr: true
Example poll:
::: {.poll #lang}
- R
- [x] Python
- Julia
:::
Deploy the server (Cloudflare with Wrangler or Docker Compose), then present with ?presenter=<key>. Data lives on your server and is exportable.
Repo: https://github.com/seandavi/quarto-revealjs-live-questions


2. Custom HTML/JS forms → your own database (Supabase, Firebase, etc.)
Full control with moderate extra work.

Drop raw HTML (buttons, radio lists, or simple forms) into a slide.
Use a small JavaScript snippet that posts votes to Supabase (or Firebase, a custom API, etc.).
Optionally subscribe to Supabase Realtime to update a chart on the slide live.
Store whatever schema you want (session ID, question ID, choice, timestamp, anonymous voter token, etc.).

This works well because Quarto RevealJS slides are just HTML. You can include external JS/CSS or write inline scripts. Services like Supabase give you a Postgres database + free tier + simple client library.


3. Existing RevealJS poll plugins (integrate into Quarto)
These are pure RevealJS plugins you can wire up via raw HTML, includes, or by treating them as custom plugins.








Plugin
Backend
Notes




jschildgen/reveal.js-poll-plugin
PHP + SQLite
Mobile voting site + API. Requires a PHP host; mark correct answers; shows bar charts. Integrate by copying the poll folder and adding the HTML markup + JS/CSS.


rajgoel seminar + poll
Socket.io server
More full-featured (seminar rooms, Q&A, etc.). Heavier setup.


anycable/slide-quiz
AnyCable (managed WebSockets) + serverless functions
Nice live quizzes/word clouds for RevealJS. Results are mostly session-only (not persistently stored for later export).



The jschildgen plugin is the closest classic “poll + SQLite database” option if you already have PHP hosting.


4. Commercial tools with embeds or QR codes

Mentimeter: You can embed an entire Menti presentation as an <iframe> inside a Quarto slide. Use data-external="1" on the iframe if you have embed-resources: true. Results stay in Mentimeter (exportable from their dashboard).
Slido, Poll Everywhere, AhaSlides, etc.: Usually show a QR code on the slide; audience votes on their phones. Results live in their system (CSV/Excel export or API). Easy to set up, but the database is theirs.



5. Local-only quizzes (no audience database)
If you only need self-contained quizzes that the presenter or individual viewers interact with (no remote voting), look at: - parmsam/quarto-quiz (and the more feature-rich quarto-learntest fork) These do not collect votes from an external audience into a database.


Recommendation by goal

Want questions in the .qmd, live results, and your own storage → start with quarto-revealjs-live-questions.
Want maximum schema control or already use Supabase/Firebase → custom HTML/JS forms.
Already have a PHP server and want a simple poll plugin → jschildgen’s RevealJS poll plugin.
Want zero hosting work → Mentimeter (or similar) embed + their export.

The live-questions extension is the closest thing to a turnkey solution that satisfies both the Quarto/RevealJS authoring style and the “results go to a database I can access” requirement. If you tell me more about your hosting preferences (Cloudflare, Docker, Supabase, etc.) or the exact poll types you need, I can sketch a more concrete setup.

Here’s a hand-held walkthrough after you’ve already run quarto add seandavi/quarto-revealjs-live-questions (so you have the _extensions/live-questions/ folder in your project).
The extension turns special divs in your .qmd into live polls/quizzes/word clouds/rating scales that talk to a small server you host yourself. Audience members scan a QR code once per talk and vote on their phones; results update live on the slide. Without a server it falls back to a plain static list (useful for PDFs).

1. Enable the extension and write questions
In your .qmd front matter (or _quarto.yml), add the extension under both filters and revealjs-plugins, plus the server settings:
---
title: "My Talk"
format: revealjs
filters:
  - live-questions
revealjs-plugins:
  - live-questions
live-questions:
  server: https://YOUR-WORKER-NAME.YOUR-ACCOUNT.workers.dev   # fill this in after step 2
  session: my-talk-2026-11-03                                 # unique name for this talk/room
---
Example questions (place them on slides):
## Which language do you use most?

::: {.poll #lang}
- R
- Python
- Julia
:::

## One word for today's lecture?

::: {.wordcloud #mood max-words=2}
:::

## Rate these statements

::: {.likert #feelings scale=agree-5}
- The material was clear
- The pace was good
:::
For quizzes, mark correct answers with task-list syntax: - [x] Correct option. Give each question an explicit #id so editing the text later doesn’t orphan old results.
Render/preview as usual (quarto preview or quarto render). Without a working server it just shows the static lists.


2. Set up a free Cloudflare Workers server (easiest for beginners)
Cloudflare’s free plan is enough. You need a free Cloudflare account and a GitHub (or GitLab) account.

Generate a long random presenter key and save it somewhere safe (you’ll need it later). On macOS/Linux:
openssl rand -hex 24
(Or use any long random string of letters/numbers/hyphens.)
Click the Deploy to Cloudflare button on the project’s GitHub README:
https://github.com/seandavi/quarto-revealjs-live-questions
(or go directly to the deploy link shown there).
Authorize it to copy the repo into your GitHub account and connect to your Cloudflare account. When it asks for the secret PRESENTER_KEY, paste the value you generated above.
Accept the suggested build/deploy commands. When it finishes, note the Worker URL (something like https://live-questions.youraccount.workers.dev or a name you chose).
Put that exact URL into your Quarto front matter under live-questions: server:.

That’s it for the server. The deploy button sets up a Worker + Durable Object that stores one “room” per session and handles WebSockets. Phones and your slides will talk to it over HTTPS.
Optional later: In the Cloudflare dashboard you can attach a custom domain (Settings → Domains & Routes) if you prefer something prettier than *.workers.dev.


Alternative: Docker (if you prefer self-hosting)
Only do this if you’re comfortable with Docker and can expose the container publicly over HTTPS (required when your slides are on HTTPS).
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seandavi/quarto-revealjs-live-questions/main/compose.yaml
curl -o .env https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seandavi/quarto-revealjs-live-questions/main/.env.example
# Edit .env and set PRESENTER_KEY=your-long-random-string
docker compose up -d
It listens on port 8787 by default. You’ll still need a public HTTPS URL that points at it (reverse proxy, Cloudflare Tunnel, etc.).


3. Present

Render or publish your slides (GitHub Pages, Quarto Pub, Netlify, etc.).
Open the deck once in the browser you’ll present from, with the key:
https://your-slides-url.html?presenter=YOUR-PRESENTER-KEY
The deck stores the key in that browser’s localStorage, removes it from the address bar, and connects as the presenter. Later visits from the same browser are automatic. Anyone else who opens the deck is a read-only viewer (they see the QR and results but can’t control anything).
Navigate to a question slide → it opens, a QR code appears, and phones can join via the session URL. Results update live.
Useful keys (presenter only):

Q – full-screen QR
A – reveal correct answer (quizzes) and close voting
T – toggle results visibility on the slide


Notes - Phones must reach the server; for real talks use a public HTTPS address. - If your slides are served over HTTPS, the server must also be HTTPS (Cloudflare Workers gives you this automatically). - Do a dry run on the machine you’ll present from. - Use ?session=rehearsal (or any other name) to practice without touching the real room. - Speaker view runs as a viewer, so present from the main window.
That’s the full path from “extension installed” to live polls. The Cloudflare button is by far the least painful option if you’re new to servers. Once the Worker is up and the server: URL is in your front matter, you’re ready to test.


How does ?presenter=YOUR_KEY work?

Here’s exactly how ?presenter=YOUR_KEY works and how to use it.


What the key does
The Cloudflare Worker has one secret: PRESENTER_KEY.
Only a browser that knows that key can control the questions (open them, close voting, reveal answers, reset, etc.). Everyone else is a read-only viewer.
The key is never baked into the HTML, so your published GitHub Pages deck is safe to share. Control is granted only by visiting with the key once.


How you use it (the practical steps)

Generate and store the key (you already did this when deploying to Cloudflare).
Example: a1b2c3d4e5f6... (the long random string you set as PRESENTER_KEY).
Become the presenter (do this once per browser/computer you will present from):

Open your published slides URL and append the key:
https://yourusername.github.io/your-repo/slides.html?presenter=a1b2c3d4e5f6...
The deck will:

Accept the key
Store it in that browser’s localStorage
Remove it from the address bar
Connect as the presenter


After that, just open the normal slides URL (no query string).
That same browser remembers it and is automatically the presenter.
Other browsers/computers, or an incognito window, will be viewers until you give them the key the same way.
To forget the key (optional):
Open https://yourusername.github.io/your-repo/slides.html?presenter= (empty value).



Walking an audience through the whole process
You can do a live demo, but a couple of practical notes:

For the audience they only need to scan the QR code that appears on a question slide. They never need the presenter key.
For you (the presenter), the key step is the one-time ?presenter=... visit. You can do that before the talk, or live in front of them if you want to show the process.
Recommended live-demo sequence:

Show the published deck URL (normal link, no key).
Explain “I’m going to become the presenter…” and open the version with ?presenter=YOUR_KEY (you can share the key on screen briefly if you’re comfortable; it’s only for this session).
Navigate to a question slide → QR code appears.
Have everyone scan it and vote.
Show the results updating live.
Demonstrate keys (A to reveal answer, T to toggle results, Q for full-screen QR) if useful.




Quick checklist before you go live with an audience

Worker is deployed and you know the exact https://….workers.dev URL
That URL is in your Quarto YAML under live-questions.server
You have the PRESENTER_KEY value written down
You have opened the deck at least once with ?presenter=YOUR_KEY on the machine you’ll present from
You’ve done a quick test vote from your phone

Once the key is stored in the presenting browser, the rest of the talk is just navigating slides normally — the questions open automatically and results stream in.

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

#' Ghost plotting function
#' @param ghost_df Data frame with x and y coordinates of the ghost shape
#' @param ghost_color Color of the ghost (default is neon green)
#' @return ggplot object of the ghost
plot_simple_ghost <- function(ghost_df, ghost_color = "#39FF14") {
  x_center <- mean(range(ghost_df$x))
  y_top <- max(ghost_df$y)
  y_bottom <- min(ghost_df$y)
  ghost_height <- y_top - y_bottom
  ghost_width <- diff(range(ghost_df$x))
  
  # Eyes
  eye_y <- y_bottom + .7 * ghost_height        
  eye_x <- x_center + c(-0.06, 0.06) * ghost_width
  eyes <- data.frame(x = eye_x, y = rep(eye_y, 2))
  
  # Mouth: several waves 
  mouth_width <- ghost_width * 0.4
  mouth_x <- seq(x_center - 0.3 * mouth_width, x_center + 0.3 * mouth_width, length.out = 80)
  mouth_y <- y_bottom + 0.55 * ghost_height + sin(seq(0, 7 * pi, length.out = 80)) * 0.04 * ghost_height
  mouth <- data.frame(x = mouth_x, y = mouth_y)
  
  # 8 neon glow layers
  glow_layers <- data.frame(
    linewidth = c(12, 10, 8, 6, 4.5, 3, 2, 1),
    alpha = c(0.04, 0.06, 0.09, 0.13, 0.18, 0.25, 0.35, 0.5)
  )
  
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_polygon(
      data = ghost_df, aes(x, y),
      fill = ghost_color, alpha = 0.15, color = NA
    )
  
  # Glow layers for outline, eyes, and mouth
  for(i in seq_len(nrow(glow_layers))) {
    p <- p +
      geom_polygon(
        data = ghost_df, aes(x, y),
        fill = NA, color = scales::alpha(ghost_color, glow_layers$alpha[i]),
        linewidth = glow_layers$linewidth[i]
      ) +
      geom_point(
        data = eyes, aes(x, y),
        color = scales::alpha(ghost_color, glow_layers$alpha[i]),
        size = glow_layers$linewidth[i] * 2.1  ## 1.1
      ) +
      geom_path(
        data = mouth, aes(x, y),
        color = scales::alpha(ghost_color, glow_layers$alpha[i]),
        linewidth = glow_layers$linewidth[i]
      )
  }
  
  # Solid black mouth and eyes
  p <- p +
    geom_path(
      data = mouth, aes(x, y),
      color = "#66ff00", linewidth = 1.2  ## with green ghost
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = eyes, aes(x, y),
      color = "#66ff00",
      size = 2
    ) 
  
  # Fix aspect ratio and theme
  p + 
    coord_fixed(
      xlim = c(-4, 4), 
      ylim = c(-3, 8), 
      expand = TRUE
    ) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA)
    )
}

#' Generate a random ghost shape
#' @param seed Optional seed for reproducibility
#' @return Data frame with x and y coordinates of the ghost shape
ghost_shape <- function(seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  width <- sample(seq(0.5, 3, length.out = 6), 1)  
  height <- sample(1:6,1) 
  x <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 100) * width
  amp <- runif(1, 0.15, 0.28)
  freq <- sample(3:7, 1)
  phase <- runif(1, 0, 2*pi)
  y_top <- sqrt(1 - (x/width)^2) * height + runif(1, -0.03, 0.03)
  y_bottom <- -0.5 * height + sin(seq(0, freq * pi, length.out = 100) + phase) * amp * height
  data.frame(
    x = c(x, rev(x)),
    y = c(y_top, rev(y_bottom))
  )
}
